correctness.rationale: For fixed r and every separately fixed J, Campbell Lemma 3 supplies J different large odd deletion sums and minimal prime partitions with r+3 members; Lemma 4 supplies three-distinct-prime alternatives; Lemma 6 with H=11 max products proves \(K(\Sigma(p)-d_i)=\pi(p)-(r+3)\) while \(L(\Sigma(p)-d_i)\ge\pi(p)-3\) for each sufficiently large prime with next gap>H. The fixed-shift two-prime upper sieve implies all but O_H(y/log^2 y) primes up to y have next gap>H. For any two distinct \(p,p^{\prime}\), their prefix sums differ by at least the larger prime; after p exceeds max differences of fixed offsets, translates have no collisions. Partial summation and PNT imply \(\pi(y_X)\sim2\sqrt{X/\log X}\) when the cumulative prime sum first reaches X, with at most one boundary exception per fixed offset. Therefore each J-template family has \((2J+o(1))\sqrt{X/\log X}\) distinct qualifying integers, and letting fixed J range arbitrarily proves the normalized count tends to infinity. No finite-sample or unproved conjecture substitutes for a step.

value.rationale: The discrepancy between the maximum number of parts and the number of parts of the maximum-product prime partition is a named exact-sum additive number theory problem. Its 2026 existence theorem offers no frequency control. The theorem determines asymptotically full prime-density witness families, explicitly counts each finite union with leading constant \(2J\) at the natural inverse-prime-prefix scale, and shows that no fixed multiple of this scale bounds the global witness counting function. This genuinely distinguishes a quantitative population theorem from arbitrary infinitude; it neither claims full asymptotics nor uniformity in r,J.
